prompt.context: Our client is an electrical utility company that had negative earnings last year due in large part to a one-time write-off of bad debt. Our client operates in what is essentially a perfectly competitive market with 30+ competitors. The way our client's industry works is this: customers typically have 12-24 month contracts and incur minimal switching costs when moving from one electrical utility company to another. Our client has brought us in for two reasons: (1) to figure out why profitability has fallen and (2) to help them improve profits going forward.
prompt.question: Why has profitability fallen, and what can the client do to improve profits going forward?

clarifying_info.q: Does our client generate its own electricity?
clarifying_info.a: No — our client does not generate its own electricity; it re-distributes it.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's price point?
clarifying_info.a: Our client charges $0.10 per kWh, which is in line with the market rate over the last few years.

clarifying_info.q: How many customers does the client serve and what is usage per customer?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently serves approximately 1 million customers per year, and that has been stable for the last several years. Demand per household has also remained steady at 1,000 kWh per month.

clarifying_info.q: What does the sign-up phase cost?
clarifying_info.a: Our client pays $50 to sign up a customer (all-in, including installation, marketing, salaries, etc.). If a customer has a low credit score, the client also collects a $100 refundable deposit.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to service a customer on an ongoing basis?
What happens when a bad customer is disconnected?
clarifying_info.a: After two months of unpaid service, the client disconnects the customer at a cost of $75. The customer may then choose to restore service (paying the two-month outstanding balance plus a $100 reconnection charge) or not. If the customer does not restore service, the client sends them to a debt collector at a cost of $50; the debt collector has a 50% success rate in collecting the outstanding payments.

exhibits.title: Customer Segmentation Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the client's customer base by customer segment (e.g., good vs. bad customers) showing the share and estimated value of each segment
exhibits.data: 50% of customers are unprofitable; 30% of customers have a value of approximately -$350 each

framework: Profitability: diagnose revenue vs. cost drivers — price, volume, and cost structure (fixed vs. variable)
Electrical Utility Market Dynamics: competitive intensity, switching costs, churn rate, contract structure
Customer Economics: customer lifetime value by segment (good vs. bad customers), acquisition costs, credit risk
Customer Segmentation: composition of customer base and how mix affects aggregate profitability
Strategic Options: levers to reduce negative-value customers and grow positive-value customers

questions.prompt: Walk through the revenue side. Has price or volume changed?
questions.guidance: Price is $0.10/kWh, in line with the market. Volume is ~1M customers at 1,000 kWh/month — both stable. Revenue changes are not the driver. Pivot attention to costs.

questions.prompt: What are the key cost drivers for this business?
questions.guidance: Strong answers structure costs into Fixed (salaries, SG&A, regulatory fees) and Variable (electricity purchase cost, marketing, installation, fees to the grid, customer acquisition costs). The candidate should identify energy costs as the largest cost driver (client earns a 10% margin on electricity transmission, so buys at $0.09/kWh and sells at $0.10/kWh). Customer acquisition cost and churn are also critical given low switching costs.

questions.prompt: Calculate the customer lifetime value (CLV) of a bad customer who chooses NOT to reconnect after disconnection. Assume the customer originally signed a two-year (24-month) contract.
questions.guidance: Candidate must independently recall the revenue figures given earlier (price, quantity) and energy cost margin (10% margin implies purchase cost = $0.09/kWh). Revenue is collected for only 22 months (last 2 months are unpaid). The deposit is kept because the customer does not return. Debt collector recovers 50% of two months of outstanding balance. All cost items: sign-up, electricity cost for 24 months, overhead for 24 months, disconnection, termination/debt-collector fee. CLV = Total Revenue - Total Costs = $2,400 - $2,503 = -$103.

math.setup: Bad customer, 24-month contract, does not reconnect. Revenue recognized for 22 months (last 2 months unpaid). Energy cost = $0.09/kWh (10% margin on $0.10/kWh price). Outstanding balance for last 2 months = $0.10 * 1,000 kWh * 2 = $200.
steps: COSTS: Electricity purchase cost = $0.09/kWh * 1,000 kWh/mo * 24 mo = $2,160
COSTS: Refundable deposit collected then returned? For bad non-reconnecting customer the deposit offsets; net cost = $100 (shown as cost in the table)
REVENUE: Expected debt collector recovery = $200 outstanding * 50% = $100
math.answer: CLV of a bad non-reconnecting customer = -$103

questions.prompt: Look at the customer segmentation exhibit. What do you notice, and what are the implications?
questions.guidance: 50% of customers are unprofitable; 30% are deeply unprofitable at approximately -$350 each. This directly explains the profitability problem. Candidate should connect the bad-customer CLV calculation to the broader customer mix issue and pivot to strategies.

brainstorming.prompt: Given that 50% of customers are unprofitable, what can the client do to improve profitability through customer segmentation?

categories.name: Increase number of positive-value customers
ideas: Reduce sign-up fee for customers with medium or above credit scores to attract more reliable customers
Introduce loyalty bonuses or rewards programs to retain good customers and reduce churn
Differentiate service through high quality or service guarantees to attract customers who value reliability
Target marketing toward customer segments with historically better payment records

categories.name: Decrease number of negative-value customers
ideas: Increase deposit requirement for customers with low credit scores
Charge a higher or non-refundable deposit for high-risk applicants
Re-examine marketing channels to reduce acquisition of high-churn or bad-pay customers
Tighten credit screening at sign-up to reject highest-risk applicants
Offer early termination fees or longer contract lock-ins to reduce churn-related losses

recommendation: Profitability has fallen primarily due to customer mix: 50% of customers are unprofitable, and 30% are deeply unprofitable at approximately -$350 each, generating a CLV of -$103 for bad non-reconnecting customers

To improve profitability, the client should (1) reduce negative-value customers by raising deposit requirements for low-credit-score applicants and tightening credit screening at sign-up, and (2) grow positive-value customers by introducing loyalty programs and reducing acquisition costs for reliable customers
risks: Raising deposit requirements or tightening credit screening may attract regulatory scrutiny in a public-utility context
Changes to customer policies could generate negative public perception or media attention
Over-aggressive screening may reduce customer volume and revenue in the short term
next_steps: Prioritize and sequence implementation: determine whether reducing bad customers or growing good customers yields faster ROI
Analyze which marketing channels are producing the highest share of bad customers and redirect spend
Model the regulatory risk of deposit/screening changes with legal and compliance teams
Quantify the NPV impact of each proposed lever to build a business case for management
